HERMOSILLO, Mexico (CNN)  -- President Felipe Calderon traveled to Hermosillo on Saturday to meet with health officials as the death toll of a day care center fire there grew to 38 children. A crib and baby seats lie outside a day care center Friday in Hermosillo, Mexico, as police cordon off the area. The cause of Friday's blaze remained unknown, but investigators concluded that the fire did not start inside the ABC Day Care, Eduardo Bours, the governor of Sonora state said. As of Saturday night, 23 children remained hospitalized, 15 of them in critical condition, Sonora spokesman Daniel Duran told CNN. Another 10 children had been transported to other hospitals: eight to Guadalajara, one to Ciudad Obregon, and one to Sacramento, California. A team of 29 medical experts in Hermosillo were deciding if any more victims would be moved to the Shriners Hospital in Sacramento, or elsewhere. In addition, six adults were injured, Duran said. "Without a doubt this is the worst disaster we've had," Bours told CNN. The president arrived with Interior Secretary Fernando Gomez Mont and Health Secretary Jose Angel Cordova to get firsthand updates from doctors and investigators, the state news agency Notimex reported. Calderon ordered the nation's attorney general to investigate the blaze. Most of the victims died from smoke inhalation and not burns, Bours said. But the fire was enough for the roof to collapse, he added. At the time of the blaze, 142 children were inside the ABC Day Care. The day care is for children ages 2 to 4, but Bours confirmed that children even younger were among the victims. All the children at the day care had been accounted for by Saturday evening, Bours said. A severely burned 3-year-old girl arrived Saturday at the Sacramento hospital -- where pediatric burn treatment is a specialty -- and was in critical condition, according to Dr. Tina Palmieri, assistant chief of the burn unit. The child was burned over 80 percent of her body, the doctor told reporters. She said the hospital normally can save just over half of the children with burns that severe. In Hermosillo, a large crowd gathered outside of the emergency entrance of the city's general hospital and many people consoled each other, video from the scene showed. "They told me that this happened in a matter of five minutes," Hermosillo Mayor Ernesto Gandara told reporters after surveying the scene.

# Day Care Fire Death Toll Rises to 38 as Mexican President Visits Scene

**HERMOSILLO, Mexico (CNN)** — President Felipe Calderón traveled to Hermosillo on Saturday to consult with health officials as the death toll from a devastating day care center fire climbed to 38 children.

A crib and baby seats remained strewn outside the day care center on Friday as police cordoned off the area. While the cause of Friday's blaze has yet to be determined, investigators have concluded that the fire did not originate inside the ABC Day Care facility, according to Eduardo Bours, governor of Sonora state.

As of Saturday night, 23 children remained hospitalized, 15 of them in critical condition, Sonora state spokesman Daniel Duran told CNN. An additional 10 children had been transferred to other medical facilities: eight to Guadalajara, one to Ciudad Obregón, and one to Sacramento, California. A team of 29 medical experts in Hermosillo was evaluating whether further victims would need to be transported to Shriners Hospital in Sacramento or other facilities. Six adults were also injured in the incident, Duran reported.

"Without a doubt, this is the worst disaster we've had," Bours told CNN.

The president arrived accompanied by Interior Secretary Fernando Gómez Mont and Health Secretary José Ángel Córdova to receive firsthand updates from doctors and investigators, according to the state news agency Notimex. Calderón has since directed the nation's attorney general to launch a full investigation into the fire.

According to Bours, the majority of victims died from smoke inhalation rather than burns—though the blaze was severe enough to cause the building's roof to collapse. At the time of the fire, 142 children were inside the ABC Day Care facility. Although the center primarily serves children ages 2 to 4, Bours confirmed that even younger children were among the victims. By Saturday evening, all children who had been present at the day care were accounted for.

A three-year-old girl with severe burns arrived Saturday at the Sacramento hospital—renowned for its expertise in pediatric burn treatment—and was listed in critical condition, according to Dr. Tina Palmieri, assistant chief of the burn unit. The child suffered burns across 80 percent of her body, the doctor told reporters, noting that the hospital typically saves just over half of children with burns of this severity.

In Hermosillo, a large crowd gathered outside the emergency entrance of the city's general hospital, with many consoling one another in scenes captured on video.

"They told me that this happened in a matter of five minutes," Hermosillo Mayor Ernesto Gándara told reporters after surveying the scene.

**HERMOSILLO, Mexico** — A devastating fire tore through a day care center in this northwestern Mexican city, killing dozens of young children and injuring dozens more in one of the deadliest disasters involving children in the country's recent history.

The blaze broke out at the ABC Day Care Center, a facility that cared for the children of workers enrolled in Mexico's national social security system, many of them employees of local businesses and government offices. Officials said the fire spread with terrifying speed through the building, trapping toddlers and infants inside as flames engulfed the structure.

Emergency crews arriving at the scene described chaotic efforts to pull children from the burning building, with parents rushing to the site as news of the fire spread through the community. Many were forced to wait in agony outside as firefighters worked to control the blaze and search for survivors.

## Death Toll Continues to Rise

Authorities said the confirmed death toll climbed steadily in the hours after the fire, with most of the victims being children under the age of 5. Health officials warned that the number could still rise, as several children remained hospitalized in critical condition with severe burns and smoke inhalation injuries.

Hospitals across Hermosillo, and even in neighboring Arizona, mobilized to treat the wounded, with some of the most severely injured children airlifted to specialized burn units for treatment unavailable locally. Doctors described grueling efforts to save young victims suffering from extensive burns covering much of their bodies.

## Cause Under Investigation

The exact cause of the fire remained unclear, though early reports suggested it may have originated in a neighboring government warehouse or an adjacent building before spreading to the day care center. Investigators were examining whether the facility met basic safety standards, including the presence of fire extinguishers, emergency exits and evacuation protocols for young children.

Questions quickly emerged about oversight of the day care center, which operated under contract with Mexico's Social Security Institute (IMSS). Critics have pointed to a pattern of privately run day care centers operating with insufficient government inspection and safety enforcement.

## Nation Mourns, President Responds

The tragedy sent shockwaves through Mexico, prompting an outpouring of grief and anger from citizens demanding accountability. Then-President Felipe Calderón addressed the nation, expressing profound sorrow over the deaths and pledging a full investigation into the circumstances that led to the fire.

"This is an enormous tragedy for all of Mexico," Calderón said, vowing that those responsible for any negligence would face justice. He ordered federal officials to work alongside state and local authorities in Sonora to determine accountability and announced that the government would cover medical expenses for all injured children.

The president also declared a period of national mourning, and flags were lowered to half-staff in a show of solidarity with grieving families across Hermosillo and beyond.

## Community in Shock

As word of the disaster spread, residents gathered outside hospitals and the charred remains of the day care center, many holding candlelight vigils for the young victims. Local officials described a community in profound shock, with counselors dispatched to support grieving families and traumatized survivors.

The tragedy has reignited calls for stricter regulation of day care facilities across Mexico, with lawmakers signaling that reforms to safety standards and inspection protocols may soon follow.
